brief.source: public Google Play Store reviews, India storefront
known_gaps: No contact volume data - review share is directional only
App reviews skew toward angry and resolved-badly customers

rounds.draft:
SUBJECT: 7.6% of negative smallcase reviews cite support

Hi {first_name},

7.6% of negative smallcase reviews on the Google Play India storefront cite the support channel failing (no response, unanswered ticket, repeated follow-up) rather than the product. It comes from 300 recent reviews fetched on 2026-10-20, so you can check it in ten minutes.

It is directional only. App reviews skew angry, this is a single snapshot, and I have no contact volume. Does it match what your ticket data shows?

I work on conversational AI for Indian BFSI support. Whether or not you reply, I can send the review quotes behind the figure, plus the 18-query eval set, including the 8 cases where a retrieval bot was confidently wrong.

{sender}
rounds.verdict: Clean on facts and offer, but 'It comes from 300 recent reviews' hides that 7.6% is a share of only 66 negative reviews, so the figure reads as sturdier than it is.
failures: Fix the denominator. 'It comes from 300 recent reviews' implies 300 is the base. The base is the 66 negative reviews among the 300 fetched (121 had substantive text). Say 'of the 66 negative reviews in 300 fetched'. Do not convert to a count of reviews, since that is a derived figure.
The small base is the caveat that most changes how 7.6% reads. 'Directional only' does not carry it, so state the 66 inline in the sentence that gives the percentage.
'Check it in ten minutes' is a promise about the reader's effort that the brief does not support. Classifying 300 reviews by hand may take longer. Say 'the reviews are public' instead.

Insight is thin. The email reports a low-ish number (smallcase ranks 7 of 19) and asks whether it matches their data. Use the brief's real angle: the complaints are about unresolved tickets, not the product. Quote one of the verbatim reviews, such as the 45-day ticket, to make that concrete.
The eval line is buried. Lead the offer with the finding that near-identical deflection rates (67% vs 72%) hid very different correctness (39% vs 94%). That is the part the recipient keeps.

rounds.draft:
SUBJECT: 7.6% of 66 negative smallcase reviews cite support

Hi {first_name},

Of the 66 negative reviews in 300 smallcase reviews I fetched from Google Play India on 2026-10-20, 7.6% cite the support channel failing rather than the product. One says: "raised issue 45 days back, TKT-143999, still no resolution."

The base is small, it is one snapshot, I have no contact volume, and app reviews skew angry. The reviews are public. Does this match your ticket data?

I work on conversational AI for Indian BFSI support. Whether or not you reply, I can send our 18-query eval set. Automation was near-identical (67% vs 72%), but correct disposal was 39% vs 94%. It includes the 8 confidently wrong cases.

{sender}
rounds.verdict: Clean on facts and caveats, with a concrete offer and no meeting ask, so it can ship, but it is a sound 3 that leans on a small stat and an eval set from other queries.
failures: Denominator is blurred: '66 negative reviews in 300' hides that the 66 come from the 121 reviews with substantive text. Say '66 negative of 121 substantive reviews (300 fetched)'. This is not a hard fail, but a hostile reader will notice.
The eval set is 18 queries from this domain, not smallcase's tickets. Say so inline, so the 67% vs 72% and 39% vs 94% figures are not read as results on smallcase.
'Whether or not you reply' reads like a sales-sequence tic. Just say 'I can send the 18-query eval set, including the 8 confidently wrong cases.'

The insight is thin. The point that a support-channel failure (a ticket that gets no reply) is a different problem from a product failure is implied but never stated. One plain sentence would make the framing land.
'Does this match your ticket data?' is a good low-friction question, but it sits between caveats and the pitch. Move it to the end so the offer is not buried.

rounds.draft:
SUBJECT: 15.7% of smallcase Play Store reviews are support-related

Hi {first_name},

15.7% of the 121 substantive smallcase reviews I pulled from Google Play India (300 fetched, 2026-10-20) are support-related. A ticket that gets no reply is a different failure from a product bug, so it is an operations problem first. One review: "raised issue 45 days back, TKT-143999, still no resolution."

It is one snapshot with no contact volume, and app reviews skew angry.

I work on conversational AI for Indian BFSI support. I can send our 18-query eval set, including the 8 confidently wrong cases. These are 18 queries from this domain, not smallcase tickets: a naive retrieval bot automated 67% and disposed 39% correctly, while routing plus system integration automated 72% and disposed 94% correctly.

Does 15.7% match your ticket data?

{sender}
rounds.verdict: Clean on facts and caveats with a real offer, but the insight is thin and the closing question asks the recipient to compare a review-share percentage against ticket data, which isn't like-for-like.
failures: The closing question 'Does 15.7% match your ticket data?' compares a share of substantive app reviews with ticket data, which measure different things. Ask something they can answer, e.g. how their ticket-unanswered cases split from product complaints.

The strongest evidence (7.6% of negative reviews cite the support channel failing) is left out. It is the figure that actually separates a ticket-resolution failure from a product complaint, and the draft instead asserts that distinction without support.
'so it is an operations problem first' is the writer's inference, not a measured finding. Soften it or tie it to the 7.6% figure.
The 18-query eval paragraph is dense and the 67/39/72/94 figures arrive in one run-on sentence. Split it or cut to the key contrast: similar automation rates, very different correctness.

'I work on conversational AI for Indian BFSI support' is generic self-description. Say what is specifically being offered and why it matters to a CX head, e.g. a bot that deflects but is confidently wrong creates more tickets like TKT-143999.
Quoting the ticket ID is verifiable but slightly exposes a customer's ticket. Consider dropping it and keeping '45 days back, still no resolution'.

rounds.draft:
FRONT_STAT: 7.6%
FRONT_LINE: of negative smallcase Play Store reviews cite the support channel failing
BACK_QUOTE: "CC is acting only as postman, raised issue 45 days back, TKT-143999, still no resolution."
BACK_BODY: Source: Google Play reviews, India, 2026-10-20. Does it match your internal picture? We build support automation; our 18-query test set and a bot's 8 confidently wrong answers are free: {short_url} {sender}
BACK_SMALLPRINT: Directional only: one snapshot, no contact volumes, reviews skew angry.
rounds.verdict: Facts are clean and the stat and quote are strong, but the back face is a cramped, jargon-heavy blob that likely breaks the 70-word limit, and the offer is garbled and arguably not even a real offer.
failures: Format: count total words across both faces. Front line (12 words incl. stat) plus quote (14), body (~35), small print (12) and URL/name lands at or above ~70. Cut to comfortably under 70, and cut the body to the 'two lines of context' the format specifies.
BACK_BODY crams source, a question, a sales pitch and an offer into one run-on. Split into two plain lines: what the number is and where it's from, then what they can get.

'our 18-query test set and a bot's 8 confidently wrong answers are free' is awkward and reads oddly: the offer is the test set and failure cases, not the wrong answers. Say e.g. 'The 18-query test set and the 8 wrong-answer cases are at {short_url}, free.'
'We build support automation' is a sales-sounding self-intro on a card meant to read as a practitioner's note. Either drop it or reduce to the sender name, and let the offer carry it.

'Does it match your internal picture?' is a mild filler question; the recipient already knows their ticket data. Consider replacing with something that frames the insight, e.g. that the complaint is the ticket channel, not the product.

The quote supports the stat directionally but is one review about one ticket; the 45-day/ticket-ID detail is checkable on Play Store but the card never tells the reader this is one of the reviews. Add 'one review:' framing in the context line.

The front line says 'cite the support channel failing' with no scope; consider 'of negative Play Store reviews' fits fine but make clear it's a share of 66 negative reviews in a 300-review sample only if word budget allows, otherwise rely on small print.

Insight is thin: the card reports a stat and doesn't surface the 67% vs 94% finding (near-identical deflection, very different correctness), which is the genuinely non-obvious point. Consider offering that as the hook.

rounds.draft:
FRONT_STAT: 7.6%
FRONT_LINE: of negative smallcase reviews cite the support channel, not the product
BACK_QUOTE: "...raised issue 45 days back, TKT-143999, still no resolution."
BACK_BODY: One review, from the Google Play India sample of 2026-10-20, so you can check it. Near-identical deflection can hide very different correctness: the 18-query test set and 8 wrong-answer cases are at {short_url}, free. {sender}
BACK_SMALLPRINT: Directional only: one snapshot, no contact volumes, reviews skew angry.
rounds.verdict: Clean and shippable: every figure traces to the brief, the caveats are in small print as the format requires, and it offers the query set. The weak point is that the bridge from the 7.6% stat to the deflection-correctness point is left for the reader to build.
failures: The base for 7.6% is the 66 negative reviews, a small sample. The small print says 'directional only' but not how few reviews sit behind the figure. Consider 'of 66 negative reviews' on the back, using a number already in the brief rather than a derived count.

The link between the quote and the sentence about deflection is implicit. Make explicit that the 18-query set shows what a bot does to a ticket like this one, e.g. 'a bot that answers wrongly here makes a 45-day ticket worse'. Stay within the brief and do not claim smallcase uses a bot.
The front does not say the source is Google Play reviews, so the stat can be read as complaint-data share. The back clarifies, but the front alone is slightly ambiguous at a glance.
'free' is a small sales tell on a card meant to read as a practitioner's note. The URL alone implies there is no cost, so consider cutting it.

The 7.6% is low in absolute terms. A hostile reader may think 'only 7.6%', and the card gives no context for why it matters. The brief's 'ranks 7 of 19' is available if you want it, but it is a mid-table rank, so only use it if it helps.
